Step-by-step reasoning

1.  Which gene is epistatic?
    •  A gene is called epistatic when its loss of function masks the phenotype of the
       mutation(s) in the other gene(s).
    •  Knock-out g2 plants show 0 % resistance, and every double mutant that carries g2
       (g1g2 and g2g3) also shows 0 % resistance, irrespective of what happens at G1 or
       G3.
    •  Therefore the g2 phenotype masks the g1 and the g3 phenotypes: G2 is epistatic to
       G1 (and to G3).

2.  Which gene is most likely the transcription factor acting upstream?
    •  A regulatory gene that acts upstream often shows only a partial loss of the final
       trait when it is knocked out, because other regulatory routes can still give some
       activity.
    •  The single mutants give: g1 = 75 %, g3 = 50 %, g2 = 0 %.  
      A complete loss (0 %) is more typical for an essential structural gene; a partial
      reduction (75 %) fits better with an upstream transcriptional regulator.
    •  Hence G1 fits best as the transcription factor; G2 and G3 behave like structural
       (pleiotropic) genes whose products are needed for resistance.

3.  Double-mutant g1g3
    •  The double mutant (10 %) is much lower than either single mutant (75 % or 50 %),
       showing that both G1- and G3-dependent branches contribute additively to the final
       resistance.  That is compatible with G1 being regulatory and G3 being another
       structural gene.

4.  Matching the interpretations with the answer options
    A)  G1 is a transcription factor; G2 and G3 show pleiotropy; G2 is epistatic toward G1
        – this matches all observations.
    B)–D) assign epistasis or the transcription-factor role in ways that conflict with the
        data (e.g. G1 epistatic over G3, or G3 epistatic over G1), so they are not
        consistent.

Therefore the only option consistent with the experimental results is option A.

Answer: A
